Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Hi everyone. I'm writing this because the other day, I was talking to
some of my Jyhad-playing friends, and we sort of came to the conclusion
that we're stuck in some kind of rut when it comes to what can be done
in Jyhad in our gaming group.

The problem, as I see it, is that the so-called metagame has become the
perhaps most important factor in determining the eventual winner of any
given game of Jyhad we play. So what I want to know is, do you out there
have a "metagame", and if so, what goes on with it? And especially, have
you solved any of the problems we have?

What I mean by the "metagame" is basically what kind of decks people design
and play, based on what they expect to be going on in a typical game of
Jyhad. Also, I'd include the aspect of what deck people actually take out
and play when starting a game of Jyhad (several of us, including me, have
multiple decks made most of the time). It seems, of late, that this metagame
has come to dominate the outcome of our games, far more than skill in either
deck construction or even game play.

The main features of our metagame include, one, an emphasis on combat. Combat
is popular here. Real popular. Seriously brutal combat decks are common
enough that most games have at least one, if not several. This has resulted
in a substantial escalation in combat/anti-combat techniques - the use of
Immortal Grapple, and to a lesser extent Hidden Lurker, Psyche, and Fast
Reaction, has become very widespread. So now, Fortitude is perhaps the
most effective combat defense - and it is so effective that it will nearly
shut down many of our mainly-potence-based combat decks. So basically,
every deck either is a serious combat deck, or else has a fair amount of
effort devoted to surviving fights with the serious combat decks.

Now, even that might not be so bad, except that I think combat has an
inherent disadvantage as a Jyhad strategy. Namely, it does not directly get
you closer to having a dead prey. Bleed does. Voting does (at least if you
use the KRC/Con Agitation type of votes). If you succeed in getting rid of
all your prey's vampires, you still have to rid him of pool, and often
enough, the only way to do that is by bleeding him for one with all your
vampires each turn. That will do the trick eventually, but in the meantime,
your predator could be killing you off right quick. So maybe you instead
send only a couple of your vampires to bleed your prey, and the others to
kick your predator's vampires into submission so you don't get ousted
yourself. That may work, but it makes combat decks really, really slow in
getting victory points.

Next, we don't seem to have any good way of dealing with weenie decks. Most
of the decks people play are not weenie decks (by weenies, I mean decks where
most if not all of the vampires have capacity one or two, maybe three).
But the weenie decks we have had have been far more effective than the
average deck - there was, a while ago, a stealth/bleed presence/obfuscate
deck that was only semi-weenie, using all vampires of cap 4 or less, and it
swept tables on a not-too-infrequent basis. The combat decks that are
prevalent here - mostly potence-based, with fortitude, celerity, or obfuscate
as secondary disciplines - are not able to effectively deal with such an
onslaught of vampires as a deck like this can put out. Weenie votes have
also caused us trouble - even with no vote push (and I suppose I've failed
to mention until now - we play no limits/golden tenets, with a few house
rules for cards we consider broken), presence-based weenie vote can almost
always pass at least a prince or two before anyone else's votes really
show up, and then they're rolling, and you can't get rid of their vampires
fast enough to stop them. I've made a deck that has three atonements in it,
which was intended largely to be able to counter such weenie decks, but the
problem there is that, one, the weenie decks are usually fast enough to
put their prey at a substantial disadvantage before s/he even gets set up,
and then, three atonements may not be enough - but more is too many, and
the blood cost is high for vamps of capacity five or less, who are the only
ones allowed to use it.

So, weenies are a problem. And the combat/anti-combat is a problem. But
the problem that they lead to is that, when we actually sit down to play
a game, the decks people pull out and where they sit seems to have an undue
influence on the outcome of the game. For example, last Friday, we played
a five-player game that turned out to be four basically-vote decks, and one
rush combat deck. The combat deck was the first one ousted. I went on
to sweep the table with my vote/bleed deck - but I don't think it was entirely
because of the brilliance of my deckbuilding and play. ;) The combat deck
was my initial prey, and he was nearly unable to hurt me, due to the great
deal of combat defense my deck had - 12 Skin of Steel, 8 Majesty - which
I know will almost never be uncalled for, since combat is so prevalent in
our group. Furthermore, my initial predator was hit hard early on by his
predator, which left him in a position of trying to recover for essentially
the entire game - and he still hadn't entirely succeeded by the time I had
ousted everyone else and come back to him, thus leaving him doomed.

What I'm looking for, then, is input as to what the experience of all the
rest of you has been in this area, and maybe even input into what we could
do toward trying to solve the problems we have here.

To give an idea of the kind of combat decks I'm talking about, here's the
one I have right now - it's a Brujah pot/cel rush combat deck, with a few
votes thrown in as my clever angle to try to give me an edge.

This deck does not always win fights, most notable against our resident

So that's it for my tirade on our local metagame. Thoughts and comments?

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
As I'm the third of this goofy meta-game wackness, I figured I'd better
say my piece as well.

I guess my main problem is that, to which most people I game with can
attest, I am not a very good strategist. I enjoy strategy games, but
I'm not that great at them.

In Jyhad, this equates to not-so-brilliant deck design. Also
contributing to this problem is my constant desire for cool combos... I
once tried to play a Dom/For/Ani deck whose main goal was to bleed on
Dawn Operations, and then use Ani retainers and combat cards to send the
blocker to torpor. It got summarily murdered by the other decks in the
group.

My current endeavors, to give everyone a good idea of the environment,
are (as mentioned) an Anti-Nossie Obf/Pot combat deck, a Toreador Tap
and Bleed deck, and a Gangrel intercept deck, which at this point is the
worst of the bunch.

The Gangrel deck sucks so much because it has no way to deal with
Fortitude and S:CE, which are present in almost all the decks in our
group (with the notable exception of Josh's Brjuah and Peter's Obf/Dom
decks). So, I rarely play the deck anymore, since it never does well.

The Anti-Nosferatu deck:

Crypt:
Lupo 2 pot Hugo 4 POT
KoKo 2 pot Agrippina 4 pot OBF
Mitchell 2 pot Nigel 5 POT obf
Duck 3 pot obf Olivia 5 POT OBF
2x Agatha 4 POT obf 2x Beast POT OBF, Bum's Rush built-in

2 Ambush
6 Bum's Rush

6 Decapitate
3 Fists of Death
4 Increased Strength
6 Torn Signpost
10 Undead Strength
8 Taste of Vitae
6 Behind You

5 Hidden Lurker
Nosferatu Kingdom
The Hungry Coyote
Shanty Town Hunting Ground
2 Minion Tap
2 Potence
4 Haven Uncovered
2 Blood Doll

80 Cards, 16% masters, 15% rush

-----------

So, that deck's pretty effective, usually with the hidden lurker action,
since I go send Mitchell to meet his doom, and Olivia was a hidden
lurker... but even then, this deck has no way to deal with Fortitude.

I my mind, Fortitude is the obvious solution to those hoping not to get
killed in combat (S:CE is easier, but also easier to deal with). No one
plays a Tremere deck, since: a) no one has both the cards and the will,
and b) you can't do unpreventable damage when you're immortally
grappled, and it's hard for the Tremere to maneuver.

So the only people who the Tremere are good against are the anti-combat
decks (and the Gangrel; yay... :( ), but they get killed by the combat
decks. The Assamites have a better chance of shaking things up, but the
only person we know with an Assamite deck can't come to our games club
meetings.

The underlying problem in my mind is that no one wants to change. We
all really like our cool combat decks. What's going to shake up our
environment? Stealth and bleed? Maybe, maybe not. There's a pretty
harsh S&B deck which plays occasionally and does fairly well, but all
the rush combat usually puts it down. Votes? Probably. The horrible 5
player game with the 4 vote decks and 1 combat deck (that was me) was
pretty harsh. Weenies? Definitely. The Obf/Pre deck (that was me,
too) was pretty effective, and had a > 50% win ratio. But it wasn't any
fun to play.

Help us out, somebody... we're in such a rut.

James

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
As further example of our groups wacky meta game action, a few weeks ago,
Josh, James Hamblin, and I were sitting around playing game after game of
3 way Jyhad. We each had 3 decks to use, so we rolled dice to see which
deck we used in each game, as well as sitting randomly. We each had seen
all of the others decks and knew what they each did.

I had a viscious Pot/For combat deck (the pre "It only works if I get out
Marty Lechtansi, v.4" deck), an Anti-Ventrue Aus/For intercept deck, and a
Nosferatu/Malk S+B+Guns deck. Josh had a Brujah Rush deck (probably the
one he posted above), a Ventrue Vote/Bleed deck, and a Toreador
Guns/Intercept. James was fielding an Anti-Nosferatu Pot/Obf rush deck
(fueled by 8 Taste of Vitae), a Pre/Cel Tap and Bleed deck (also recently
posted), and a Gangrel Intercept/Blood gain deck.

In all of the 5 or 6 games we played in rapid sucession, we were
succsessfully able to predict the winner of every game, based entirely on
what decks we were using and where we were sitting at the time. For
instance, if Josh was my Predator with his Ventrue deck, I was playing my
Pot/For combat deck, and James was my prey with his Gangrel deck, Josh
would win, and we all knew it was going to happen. On the other hand, if
Josh, James and I were in the same table posititons and used the same
decks, except that James used his Tap and Bleed deck instead of the
Gangrel one, he would win. If all three of us were playing our combat
decks (Brujah, Anti-Nos, Mixed Pot/For), I would win. Invariably. It was
wacky.

We rotate decks within limits (usually everyone has at least one new deck
every week, and then the other two or three are the same), and there are 2
or 3 other people who play with us regularly, but still, we can pretty
much look at who is playing with what deck in what postiton in any
particular game, and pretty much know who will win from the beginning
(this becomes less likely with the more people who play in any particular
game). When we do make new decks, the whole meta aspect gets out of
control, as you try real hard to not specifically make decks to kill your
friends deck, as that would be wack, but still trying to make a sucessful
deck, knowing what is likely to be in any particular game.

Just the other day, James was thinking of making a new Nosferatu Obf/Ani
combat deck, but he said "What is the point. It'll get whacked by all the
other Immortal Grapple powered combat decks and will be unable to deal
with the S:CE or Fortitude of the other anti-combat decks. Eech."

Eh. What can you do.

I find the metagame evolves - when everybody has oodles of combat defense,
people will stop playing (many) combat decks. If people in your group
like combat so much they play combat decks even if they have little
chance, then the problem is that you are *not* playing the metagame.

We don't have much of a problem with ruts, but then we all have
significant variety of basic types and pretty much all value innovation.

As to the predator/prey situation, yes, that can be a problem. Some
people play better than others; some prefer defensive play and some
offensive. I've seen a fair number of games decided by
fortunate/unfortunate table position. This problem doesn't kind of
disappear on its own, like the rut problem. So that you personally don't
contribute to the problem, my recommendation is that you play decks with
both good offense and good defense.

Hello! Sombody else from their playgroup breaking in here. I
think you've hit the nail on the head here: the biggest problem is
trying to combine playing "for fun" and playing "to win" at the same
time. This is a big problem in most multi-player games. In a setting
where there is no extra incentive to win (such as prizes of some
sort), some people prefer to use stategies ( and in CCG's this means
use decks) that focus on maximizing their own personal fun. This
sounds great, and is, if everyone is doing it. Unfortunately, when
some but not all of the people playing are doing this, and the others
are really attempting to win, then it is really frustrating for the
latter group, because they are forced to deal with people playing
irrationally. The most common example of this is when one player
decides to help another win. In games like L5R and Illuminati, this
generally means that the person wins. In Jyhad, this is not as common

winning. Prizes jump immediately to mind, of course, but that would
have to be prohibitively expensive to be worth while. Ante could

anyway, or play for useful/rare cards, and people who lose are often
badly hurt by the loss. The best idea I've had up to this point would
be to keep some kind of rankings list. It wouldn't be to hard to do
(providing we could agree on how it would work...), and, in my
experience, stuff like that increases desire to win by more than you
would think.

When you rebuild one of your favorite decks, take into account what

a weak position. If you do this, you will be playing the metagame

give your friends a little shove, once in a while, if they become

Sun again:

Use more deception in your games. Sacrifice a small vampire,

into your decks.

Then rebuild it with first strike/aggro damage to complement the
intercept, instead of Majesty/Dodge.

This method tends to have a number of benefits. As you describe,
people's decks tend to be more balanced and less chosen for their ability
to deal with specific decks. Another bonus is that games tend to be
harsher. Since players aren't going to be directly prepared for each
specific deck, more conflict tends to occur. This earlier conflict
causes an acceleration of games that let's more games get played, but
also increases a deck's ability to survive in a harsh environment. I'm
sure you'll find that playing in another environment (a tourney for
example), groups with random seating will have a much higher incidence of
success in these environments.

I think that the matter may have been beaten nearly into torpor, but I
have already played "Opening the Mouth" and have to get my swing in

If your play group tries to use STYLE in deck building, the game is a
lot more fun. In my group, there are 4-7 people per week playing. Of
that group, two of us usually try to bring a new concept deck at least
every other week. The other players change more sporadically, or are

I'm not talking about the new and improved sneaky bleed deck here, we

amusing to see that bleed bounce from Methuselah to Methuselah. And

Lets face it, not everyone has the time or inclination to build cool

On Thu, 13 Feb 1997, Robert Goudie wrote:

[Re: Ranking Players to make more of a sense of competition]

> This is a great idea. Ok, let's start brainstorming about some systems
> for ranking players.

This season's Madison Jyhad League is an Open Season (play sealed,
constructed, whatever you want...), but we score games as follows.

1) Each Player starts with 1000 points. Players can start at any time.

2) Whenever a league game happens, each player throws 10% of their
current point total into the Victory Pool.

3) Each player gets a fraction of the Victory Pool equal to the fraction
of Victory Points they received. (i.e., 4 player game, winner with 3VP
gets 75% of pool).

It works quite well and is relatively simple to explain and implement.
To keep people from getting discouraged, it is important to note that
800-1200 is still about "average".

(I got really lucky this Wednesday when I picked up 6VP in a 7 Player
Game... :)

Good luck. It kind of increases rivalry, but hasn't seemed to increase
player tension, but YMMV.

James Hamblin wrote:
"I've tried to re-gear my decks to primarily play to win, and I think that
it'd be a lot better for everyone involved if we all played to win.
Unfortunately, the big problem is weenie decks. They're always going to
be successful, so do we disallow them?"

Now when everyone says "we want people to play to win" what do they mean?
Do we want people to not play decks that have no chance of winning or do
we want people to make as killer decks as possible? There is a large
difference there. What is the difference between playing a deck that
can't actually win (i.e. get the most victory points) and playing a newly
designed untested deck idea that may end up being bad? How do you
determine wheither someone is playing to win or not?

When I make decks, I try to build decks that can win games. Some of them
are much better than others at doing that, but I don't make decks that are
designed to lose. Granted, sometimes my decks main way of ousting its
prey is to bleed them one point at a time, but even that works sometimes.
All the decks I own have some possiblity of winning somewhere in them, and
when I play I attempt to oust my prey. What else defines trying to win?

If we intend on making as killer decks as possible (i.e. "I'm playing to
win!"), then we are all going to end up with high speed weenie decks, at
least for a while, until everyone starts making anti weenie decks. If
there is a limit on "weenie decks", then everyone will end up with as
close to said "weenie deck" as possible in the realm of the rules.

What do you mean by "...deck tinkering."? Why would we not allow deck
tinkering? I'm confused by that. How do you regulate "deck tinkering"?

How do you regulate wheither a deck is "too good" and needs to be retired?
That is just silly. If we intend on making as killer winning decks as we
can, what is the point of doing that if someone is going to say "Oh boy.
You certainly swept the table 4 times with that weenie bleed deck. We're
impressed. Play something new now." If the whole point is to play to
win, why punish someone for winning? That does not make sense.

Messages.Body:
PDB6 (pd...@aol.com) wrote:

: "I've tried to re-gear my decks to primarily play to win, and I think that

: determine wheither someone is playing to win or not?

Hi Peter, James, Steve. Before I get into the ranting and raving bit, I'll
just say that I like Adrian Sullivan's scoring system too, and think we
should use that one if we want to start using a score system.

Now for the ranting...

There is no such thing as a deck that has no chance of winning. Any deck
can get the most victory points by making one vampire and bleeding its prey
for one every turn until s/he dies, and then its next prey, and so on. I
know, that's not what you mean, but there's as big a difference between
"no chance of winning" and "slim chance of winning" as there is between decks
that "can't win" and that are "as killer as possible."

: When I make decks, I try to build decks that can win games. Some of them

: are much better than others at doing that, but I don't make decks that are
: designed to lose. Granted, sometimes my decks main way of ousting its
: prey is to bleed them one point at a time, but even that works sometimes.
: All the decks I own have some possiblity of winning somewhere in them, and
: when I play I attempt to oust my prey. What else defines trying to win?

See, that's the problem with the idea of decks that can't win games - any
deck can win a game; it's all a matter of degree whether it has nearly no
chance of doing so, as opposed to a great chance of sweeping the entire
table.

Every deck anyone plays, and any deck anyone has ever played in our group,
has an ability to win. There are decks that will in practice never win games,
for example an intercept combat deck that never bleeds its prey and has no
other way of causing its prey to lose pool - such a deck, while it may often
get two victory points, for being the last person alive and ousting its last
surviving opponent, will never outright win a game of four players or more.

What I think James probably means by playing to win (and what I mean by
playing to win) is that you're playing a deck that you believe is designed
to garner as many victory points as possible. That hypothetical intercept
combat deck would not be designed to win, in this sense.

: If we intend on making as killer decks as possible (i.e. "I'm playing to

: win!"), then we are all going to end up with high speed weenie decks, at
: least for a while, until everyone starts making anti weenie decks. If
: there is a limit on "weenie decks", then everyone will end up with as
: close to said "weenie deck" as possible in the realm of the rules.

Okay, at this point I feel obliged to point out that we felt exactly the
same way, a year ago, about playing in a no-card-limits environment. The
argument then was that everyone would end up playing decks in the style of
a 20 majesty/20 kine resources contested/20 bewitching oration deck. We
were wrong about that. Maybe we're also wrong that weenie decks (by which
I mean decks that don't make any substantial use of vampires of capacity
greater than three; the ideal weenie deck would use only 1s and 2s) would
dominate an environment in which everyone was really playing "to win" - a
more cutthroat environment, where people really tried to get all the VPs
they could.

Or, maybe you're right, and weenie decks are inherently the most efficient
decks in Jyhad. I know there are at least a couple groups out there that
really do play speedier, more "to win" decks - is it your experience, folks,
that it's all weenies out there?

: What do you mean by "...deck tinkering."? Why would we not allow deck

: tinkering? I'm confused by that. How do you regulate "deck tinkering"?

I think James probably was thinking of deck tinkering in the milieu of us
playing with a scoring system like the one Steve and Adrian S. referred to.
Maybe he was thinking that we would be essentially playing a sort of ongoing
tournament, and as such, playing only one deck (?) and not messing with it
during the scoring period, or some such.

It's not what I was thinking of though - I was thinking that people would
have scores, rather than decks having scores, and as such they would score
points for the games they play, regardless of what deck they're playing, or
how altered it is from the last time they played it.

: How do you regulate wheither a deck is "too good" and needs to be retired?

: That is just silly. If we intend on making as killer winning decks as we
: can, what is the point of doing that if someone is going to say "Oh boy.
: You certainly swept the table 4 times with that weenie bleed deck. We're
: impressed. Play something new now." If the whole point is to play to
: win, why punish someone for winning? That does not make sense.

There is no point to retiring decks for being too good, if you've decided
that playing "to win" is where it's at. But I don't know that we've decided
that, and I don't even know if we're going to.

However, saying things like "Gosh, that weenie deck sure is effective. Why
don't you put it away and play a real deck now?" is something we *do*, and
it's something we've been doing for a while now. Basically, we still have
a set of unwritten house rules, besides the card-based ones we actually have
written down. They say something like "Weenie decks are classless and too
effective, so you shouldn't use them. Offensive votes are too effective and
no one wants to use sufficient defense against them, so the entire table is
justified in voting against them or otherwise stopping them. Combat is fun
and classy, so people are allowed to play rush combat (or other such) decks
even if the only way they will ever oust anyone is by sending all their prey's
vampires to torpor and then bleeding them for a one a turn with all their
vampires till their prey is dead."

I don't think it's good for our play group, or for anyone's peace of mind,
to have unwritten rules like that. I think if we want to have rules limiting
the effectiveness of allowable decks - for example, disallowing weenie decks
cause we don't want our "cool" decks to lose to them every time we play -
we should admit that we have such rules, and write them down.

Okay, that's probably enough tirade for now. I had been considering doing
a from-scratch rant on this, but since you saved me the trouble, Peter, I
won't have to do that now. ;) So, thoughts anyone?

Josh

First off - I like the playgroup ranking idea, but its value might be
questionable given the wide disparity in group talent and dedication
levels. Weak groups will have one or two players with artifically
high totals. Sure, they can only go so far, since the returns
diminish as they beat the same people over and over again. But a
fairly weak player with one (or more) good deck could easily
accumulate several times his starting total if he never left his (very
weak) playgroup. This should be addressed, but I'm not sure how yet.
Cross-pollenation is the obvious, but difficult solution

And I would suggest implementing a deck-replay restriction of some
type.

Only play a deck X times,
or you cannot play the same deck X times in a row,
or you must randomly select from a deck collection of at least X
(different) decks.

That will help to allay some peoples concerns and will discourage
stagnation.

Now - for some other topics:

>"I've tried to re-gear my decks to primarily play to win, and I think that
>it'd be a lot better for everyone involved if we all played to win.
>Unfortunately, the big problem is weenie decks. They're always going to
>be successful, so do we disallow them?"

snip

>If we intend on making as killer decks as possible (i.e. "I'm playing to
>win!"), then we are all going to end up with high speed weenie decks, at
>least for a while, until everyone starts making anti weenie decks. If
>there is a limit on "weenie decks", then everyone will end up with as
>close to said "weenie deck" as possible in the realm of the rules.

Sure, I'll agree that weenie decks are very effective, especially if
your entire table uses them. But I think you'll find that there are a
number of viable, winning solutions to the weenie problem, and there's
no need to be intimidated unless your deck is unstructured or depends
on slow combos.

For example - anything that allows direct attacks on vampires,
especially as a global, continuing effect is tremendously effective at
eliminating the weenie horde and controlling the table - especially if
you have untap effects. You can wack several minions in a turn without
only minimal damage. And if they are packing SCE to avoid your
combat, the have altered the heavy bleed component, so the deck is
slow or dilute enough to control,

And as soon as you off a few of those weenies, most horde bleeders get
stuck playing defensively, since they have no highly efficient pool
engine. Another slowing factor.

In last weekend's tournament, my Nosferatu (yes - I played ugly guys
throwing sewer lids and cars in a tournament) deck stopped a weenie
steath vote deck and weenie dom bleed deck (sorry Robert). I had
watched both those decks sweep tables, but they were held in check
with Beast and a few Forced Awakenings. And beast is easy to get out
in the 2nd round (7 capacity)

The biggest thing that kept the combat deck from controlling the table
was a well-constructed Minion Tap/Golconda/Soul Gem pool engine
sitting as its prey - another 7-10 blood minion deck. It couldn't
keep the minions down, or develop enough pool to stay even. The pool
engine eventually took the tournament.

So please don't complain that weenie vote or bleed decks are just too
fast to stop. It can be done easily and you don't even need to focus
on weenie-stopping. Just take a chance and explore some new deck
combinations.

It's not at all impossible. There are three basic defenses for S&B:
intercept the bleed, bounce the bleed (deflection or Telepathic
Misdirection), or rush the bleeders (Bum's Rush or Haven uncovered, thebn
torporize the target). You can also extend your life with blood gain or
outrace the bleeder and oust your prey first (with a weenie bleed or fast
aggressive vote deck).

A couple of points:

If you aren't playing intercept, *don't* intercept his bleeds. Ever.
You'll never block them; all you'll do is use his stealth cards so he
draws more bleed cards and bleeds you for more.

Use defense techniques which are uncommon in your group. If everybody
plays intercept, use rush; if everybody plays rush use intercept (bounce
always works, though).

Everybody can defend vs. S&B. However, it does take up a lot of your
deck. With any deck I build the #1 question and the #1 use of cards is my
deck's offensive goal; but my defense for S&B is almost always #2.

>For the most part no one plays with this kind of deck
>cause its frowned upon ( its the easiest deck to make, takes no

Weenie bleed is easier to make, but takes a little more guts as you lose
